conversations.content:
Task: Competition Tiebreaker Problem Solving
1. Problem Details:

* Problem Document: https://oceanbase.yuque.com/org-wiki-obtech-vh7w9r/hc3pio/vzt7rbh4125g18wx (contains 2 tiebreaker tasks)
* Baseline Repository: https://github.com/oceanbase/seekdb/tree/2026-competition-round2

2. Objective:

* Solve both tasks aiming for a 100% full score.
* Implement optimized, robust, and competition-ready solutions as quickly as possible.

3. Questions & Workflow:

* How should we set up the environment and collaborate? Should I clone the repo locally and share the relevant files/diffs, or how do you suggest we proceed?
* Can you access the problem link directly? (If not, let me know and I will paste the problem specifications here).

Please outline the step-by-step execution plan first.

Read the Yuque pages with a browser (plain fetch only returned the title). The tiebreaker section holds one problem (MiniVectorDB, built from scratch) plus the scoring rules; the two 40-point items are a performance ranking and an Agent-prompt ranking, both gated on passing every hidden MySQL case. Points come from rank, so a fixed 100% is not something any team can guarantee. The round-2 branch has the seekdb engine deleted and empty Dockerfile/conversation.json placeholders; the official test driver and problem package were not published yet. Proposed phases: setup, correct engine, own differential/crash test harness, adapt to the driver, performance, submission.

Rust

1. Urgency & Competitive Strategy:
   * Speed is everything. In this tiebreaker, ranking is determined by whoever achieves a full score first. We are competing in real-time against other teams using Agents. We are NOT waiting for the deadline; we need to achieve 100% full score as fast as humanly possible.
2. Language Choice:
   * Let's use Rust. A single crash gives an immediate 0 score, so Rust's memory safety gives us the highest reliability while maintaining raw C-level performance and SIMD capabilities.
3. Repo & System Permissions:
   * Authorized: Go ahead and push upstream's 2026-competition-round2 branch to zhangxh0526/seekdb and clone it directly into /home/legend/project/oceanbase.
   * I have installed Docker / am ready to execute any setup commands.
4. Execution Protocol:
   * Skip unnecessary pleasantries. Immediately start Phase 0 (Setup) and Phase 1 (Core Engine & Storage) right now.
   * Keep the architecture modular and stdin/stdout protocol layer lightweight so we can instantly wire it to the official test driver the minute it drops.
   * For agent/conversation.json, pause briefly only at critical architectural forks with clear A/B choices or tricky edge-case validations so I can steer and record the required evidence without blocking your coding speed.

Let's begin right now: push the branch, set up the repo skeleton, and write the minimal SQL parser & page storage.

Asked an A/B question on storage. A: append-only log that is also the table store, one checksummed frame per commit plus fdatasync, in-RAM primary-key index, recovery truncates the torn tail. B: page-based B+tree with buffer pool, redo WAL and checkpoints. Agent recommended A.

I choose Option A: Log-structured.
Here is my architectural rationale and key constraints we must adhere to:

1. Zero-Crash Guarantee: B+Tree with ARIES recovery is prone to corruption and segfaults during edge-case splits or buffer eviction. With the competition rule stating "a single crash gives an immediate 0 score", Log-structured is vastly superior because recovery is trivially idempotent (just scan records and truncate torn tail).
2. Optimal I/O Score: In Option A, data is written exactly once (WAL IS the data log), whereas B+Tree writes twice (WAL + Page flushing). This gives us a major competitive edge in the 20% disk I/O scoring weight.
3. Critical Trap to Prevent (Hidden Test OOM):
   * You noted that hidden tests will exceed container RAM. Therefore, we CANNOT keep all raw vectors permanently cached in RAM.
   * Keep the PK index in RAM (PK -> file offset is very compact, ~16 bytes/row).
   * For TopK vector scans: implement a streaming reader (read in chunks of e.g. 64KB/128KB with SIMD distance calculation) instead of loading the whole dataset into RAM.
   * Remember: Peak container memory includes OS PageCache. After flushing or large sequential scans, advise the OS via posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) so the kernel file cache doesn't inflate our memory footprint.

Proceed with Option A immediately. Start with scaffolding the crate, the lexer, and the append-only log engine!

Agreed with A and raised one problem with the scan plan: in the benchmark the whole vector set is about 10,000 x 128 x 4 B = 5 MB; if every one of the 1,000 queries streams it from disk after DONTNEED dropped the cache, that is about 5 GB of physical reads, which the I/O metric counts. Proposed instead: keep a compact in-memory copy while a table fits a memory budget, stream with DONTNEED only above it; on the write path drop pages after fdatasync except the partial last page, which the next append would otherwise read back. Also noted that the rules rank the final version at the deadline by the performance metric and do not break ties by submission time.

Yes, please commit this scaffold first, and then proceed directly with the executor. Do not worry about Docker for now—we will test the Docker build later.
Proceed with:

1. Commit the current passing code with a clean commit message.
2. Implement the Executor (table catalog, in-memory PK index, streaming TopK with SIMD distance, transactions with BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK and statement-level undo).
3. Start the differential test harness against the Python reference model.

Let's keep moving!

Docker is now installed and verified. Please commit the current scaffold first, and then proceed with the executor and test harness.

Committed the scaffold, then built the executor: per-table primary-key index into the log plus a row cache (vectors packed contiguously) while under a memory budget of a quarter of the cgroup limit, else rows are read from the log. Every statement writes to a transaction overlay with an undo list; a failed statement replays its undo; COMMIT writes the overlay as one log frame. Where the task text is silent it followed MySQL: DDL and BEGIN implicitly commit. Other open choices (to check against the official package): UPDATE SET values are validated even if no row matches; number/string comparisons are type errors; unordered results come in pk order. Wrote tests/difftest.py: random sessions compared against a Python reference model, with an optional kill -9 mode. Vector components are multiples of 1/4 so both sides compute distances exactly and tie-breaking by pk is tested without float noise.

Start performance

The progress is fantastic, and all four architectural decisions (DDL autocommit, strict type checking, no implicit string conversions, and PK order) are fully approved.
Let's start the Performance Phase:

1. Implement hand-written AVX2 SIMD routines for the 128-dimensional L2 distance calculation to minimize query latency.
2. Build the benchmark harness to measure execution time, cgroup peak memory (memory.peak), and disk I/O (io.stat), verifying our earlier prediction on posix_fadvise page cache savings.

Let's sprint for the top performance score!

Built bench/bench.py after the spec's section 3.3 (write phase from an empty table, 100 rows per commit; cold restart, warmup, 1,000 TopK queries, half filtered). Each phase runs in its own systemd user unit to read memory.peak from a real cgroup; this machine's user manager has no io controller, so I/O comes from /proc/<pid>/io, not io.stat. Added an AVX2/FMA float32 kernel used only as a prefilter: a row gets its exact f64 distance only if a proven error bound says it could still enter the TopK, so results stay identical to an exact scan. The fadvise prediction held for the write phase but not for the query phase, where peak memory is reached during recovery, before the old end-of-replay drop; recovery now drops pages as it reads. One mistake on the way: the first re-measurement ran a stale release binary (cargo test does not rebuild it) and showed no change; the harness now refuses a binary older than the sources.

I choose Option A: Columnar in-memory cache.
Here is the architectural reasoning for conversation.json:

1. Zero-Crash Rule vs. SIGBUS Hazard: Option B (mmap) introduces severe SIGBUS crash hazards if files are truncated, rotated, or recovered under unexpected signals. Given the competition's strict rule that a single crash zeroes the score, we cannot afford any unsafe mmap failure modes. Safe, managed Rust data structures are strictly required.
2. Eliminating the 23 ns Scan Overhead: The profiler identified ~23 ns/row of non-arithmetic overhead (pointer indirection, heap headers, B-tree traversal). A columnar layout (Structure of Arrays) packs vector floats into contiguous, aligned memory chunks, giving optimal L1/L2 prefetching and eliminating per-row pointer chasing.
3. Filter Pushdown Advantage: Since 50% of benchmark queries have equality filters, the columnar layout allows us to scan the compact filter column first. Filter-rejected rows completely avoid reading the 512-byte vector into cache lines, minimizing memory bus bandwidth.
4. README Clarification: Yes, recording my approval covering the README's second item (strict validation regardless of matching rows) is correct.

Please commit the current AVX2 and benchmark work first, and then proceed with implementing Option A (Columnar Cache). Let's see the new query benchmark numbers!

Corrected two points of c11 before building: no profiler was used (perf was unavailable; the ~23 ns/row came from timing unfiltered queries against the kernel benchmark), and filter-rejected rows already skipped the vector before this change. Built the columnar cache (pk and int arrays, one string buffer with spans, packed vectors, slot reuse) and slot-order scans for TopK and ORDER BY. First A/B: memory as estimated (-1.3 MiB) but query time only -10% instead of the estimated ~2.6x; timing by query type showed the B-tree walk and per-row pointers had been cheap (rows allocated in order) and the generic filter evaluation was the real cost. Then added filter pushdown: simple column-constant conditions run as loops over the column arrays and produce a slot list. A crash test failure (seed 825) turned out to be a harness bug present before this change: an index changes no rows, so the crash check could not tell whether a CREATE VECTOR INDEX survived; it now probes by repeating the statement.

Yes, please commit the columnar cache and the difftest fix immediately.
Reflection & Strategic Next Steps:

1. Results Evaluation: 310.7 ms for 1,000 TopK queries (~0.31 ms/query ) with 6.77 MiB peak memory and Recall=1.0 is fantastic.
2. Trade-off on ANN vs. Exact Scan: Before jumping into an ANN index (e.g. IVF or HNSW), let's carefully evaluate the trade-off: 10k rows is only ~5 MB. An ANN index incurs extra memory footprint (which directly penalizes the 20% peak memory score), extra restart/rebuild time during cold starts, and recall risk (<1.0). Is ANN actually net-positive for the total composite score E, or does our 0.31 ms exact AVX2 scan already dominate?


1. Write-Path Optimization: Since write profiling showed ~0.18s spent on SQL lexing/parsing and conversion (vs. 0.08s for fsync), can we optimize the parser hot-path (e.g., fast float/vector parsing, avoiding heap allocations during INSERT)?
2. Docker Verification: Since Docker is installed, let's also run a smoke test on the Dockerfile to ensure the container builds and runs cleanly as specified by the grader.

Please commit the current work and outline the next optimization targets!

Committed a8ab4d4. ANN vs exact: a floor run (the same 1,000 queries with a primary-key condition that matches nothing) took ~45 ms against ~313 ms exact, so ~85% of query time is the scan an index could shorten. A k-means IVF probe (100 lists) showed the answer depends on the data: on uniform data recall stays below 0.95 until most rows are scanned, so there is nothing to gain; on 50 Gaussian clusters, 4 lists (4% of rows) gave recall >= 0.99 with and without the filter at all three spreads tried. An exact variant (stop once the triangle-inequality bound of the next list exceeds the current 10th distance) scanned 2-4% of rows with recall exactly 1.0 when clusters were tight (sigma 0.15, 0.3), and fell back to a full scan on uniform data and at sigma 0.5. Such an index costs ~0.1 MiB (51 KB of centroids, 40 KB of list ids) against a 6.8 MiB peak, so by the scoring formula the time gain dominates on clustered data; the choice waits for the published distribution. Corrected one point of c13: the ~0.18 s was the whole user CPU of the write workload in an earlier timing, not a profile; lexing and parsing alone took ~0.10 s, and vector literals are converted to floats later, at bind time. Docker: the daemon has no proxy and could not reach Docker Hub, so the two pinned base images were fetched through the shell's proxy by a script that checks every blob digest, then loaded with their pinned digests; the Dockerfile built unchanged and tests/docker_smoke.sh passed. Inside the container io.stat equals /proc/<pid>/io, but times are higher: each statement round trip through docker's stdio relay costs ~90 us more (floor 136 vs 45 ms), and the same binary uses more CPU per query (0.35-0.37 vs 0.29 s). A native probe that leaves the process idle between queries also raised its CPU per query, which fits an idle-core penalty but does not prove it is the whole cause.

Let's start with Target 1: Write Path Optimization.
Rationale & Guidance:

1. Data-Agnostic Certainty: The write workload (10k rows × 128-dim vectors, 100 rows/commit) is fixed regardless of vector distribution. Shaving CPU time from the current 0.18s down towards the ~0.08s fsync physical bound is guaranteed performance gain with zero algorithmic risk.
2. Execution Focus:
   * Optimize vector and float parsing: use a fast-path zero-copy parser for float literals in vector arrays (avoiding intermediate string allocations and standard library parsing overhead).
   * Minimize row copies and intermediate heap buffers during INSERT batching into the columnar table.
3. Follow-up Milestone:
   * As soon as the write path hits the ~200 ms target, let's proceed immediately to Target 2: Exact IVF with Triangle Inequality Pruning. Real-world embeddings (e.g. OpenAI/BERT/CLIP representations) inherently exhibit strong semantic clustering rather than uniform hyper-spherical randomness. An exact IVF that achieves 20x scan reduction on clustered data while falling back safely with Recall=1.0 is an unbeatable architecture for the query phase.

Please proceed with the write-path optimizations and show the new write benchmark numbers!

Measured before changing anything: the write workload run in-process stage by stage (e25). Two costs had not been expected in c14: every statement was tokenized twice, once only to check whether it was blank (32 ms), and the statement splitter walked quoted text one byte at a time (36 ms). Changes: the blank check skips whitespace and comments only; quoted text is searched eight bytes at a time in the splitter and the lexer; string literals move from tokens into the syntax tree instead of being cloned; vector literals are parsed in one pass, with Clinger's exact fast path (significand <= 2^24, decimal exponent <= 10 in magnitude, one float32 multiply or divide) and the old parser for anything else, checked bit for bit against str::parse::<f32> on 200,000 random decimals. Corrections to c16: fsync time is waiting, not CPU, so the two add up instead of CPU shrinking toward the fsync time; and the parser is not zero-copy (each statement is still copied into the splitter and into its own string, each literal once into its token), but the copies were never the cost. Result (e26): write T 297.5 -> 150.9 ms (median of five), CPU 0.21 -> 0.07 s, peak memory 7.54 -> 7.28 MiB, bytes written unchanged; in the container 377.5 -> ~170 ms. What remains is mostly the 100 fdatasync calls (~0.8 ms each). A crash seed failed the same way on the previous build: a crash during CREATE TABLE inside an open transaction can keep the transaction's commit without the table, because the implicit commit is its own log frame (the approved DDL autocommit rule); the checker now accepts that state (e27). On c16's point 3: the benchmark data comes from the task's own generator, whose distribution is still unpublished, and in e20 exact pruning already stopped working at sigma 0.5 while 4 probed lists still found the true neighbours; exact IVF is safe (recall 1.0, ~1% extra work when nothing is pruned), but its gain on the real benchmark is unknown until the distribution is.

Target 2 of c16, exact IVF. About sqrt(n) k-means lists over the cached vector column (32 training rows per list, 10 rounds, deterministic); each list keeps a padded upper bound on its members' distance to the centroid. A TopK visits lists by the lower bound |q - c| - radius, with |q - c| taken from the float32 kernel through its proven error bound, and stops when the bound exceeds the K-th exact distance, so results equal a full scan, ties included. Inserts, updates and deletes keep the lists current. The index is built during recovery, on CREATE VECTOR INDEX, or before a TopK-shaped SELECT once a table has 4,096 rows, rebuilt when the table doubles, and never during the write phase. The first measurement found a regression (e29): where nothing can be pruned (uniform data, sigma 0.5) visiting rows list by list was about 1.6x slower than the slot-order scan, because a list's rows were scattered in memory. Fix: when the index is built the cached rows are moved so each list is contiguous, the vectors permuted in place so peak memory does not grow. Five-round medians after that (e30): uniform 305.4 -> 315.3 ms, 50 clusters at sigma 0.15 309.5 -> 49.5 ms, sigma 0.3 288.9 -> 50.6 ms, sigma 0.5 287.4 -> 305.1 ms; recall 1.0 in every run, peak memory unchanged, write phase unchanged, recovery about 60 ms longer for the build. Tests (e31): unit tests for the bounds and for indexed TopK against offering every row (ties, filters, updates and deletes after the relayout); the differential and crash tests with the index forced onto every table, which also caught a deliberately loosened bound. The clustered workloads are synthetic and chosen by the agent: whether the task's data is clustered tightly enough for the bound to prune is still unknown.

experiments.purpose: Does an IVF index keep Recall@10 >= 0.95 while scanning few rows? tests/ivf_probe.rs: 10,000 x 128 rows, k-means with 100 lists, 300 queries, every other one filtered to 1 of 10 categories; recall against an exact scan for each number of probed lists. Uniform data as in the bench, then 50 Gaussian clusters of three spreads. Last line of each block: an exact variant that visits lists by the triangle-inequality bound |q - c| - radius(c) and stops once it exceeds the current 10th distance, so its results equal a full scan. The task's real distribution was not yet published.

limitations: Clustered benchmark data (bench.py --clusters) is a synthetic Gaussian mixture chosen by the agent; the task's own data distribution was not published at the time of writing.
The wire format, error codes and ready marker are placeholders; the official test driver was not published at the time of writing.
Benchmarks ran on one desktop machine (i5-9400F, NVMe ext4), mostly outside Docker with I/O from /proc/<pid>/io; inside Docker (e23) io.stat gave the same byte counts.
The Docker base images were fetched by a script through a local proxy (e22) because the Docker daemon on this machine cannot reach Docker Hub; the grading environment pulls them itself.
The reference model was written from the same reading of the task as the engine, so it finds implementation bugs but cannot catch a shared misreading of the rules.

Filter pushdown and the benchmark cover one filter shape (string equality over 10 categories); other conditions take the generic per-row path, and SELECT without ORDER BY still walks the primary-key index.
